title: Formal and informal language for an audience
blurb: Read the purpose, audience and occasion of any message, then pick the register that fits: formal, informal or plain language.
question: An applicant needs to email the admissions director to ask for a two-day extension on a transcript deadline. Her draft starts, “Hey! So my college is being super slow with transcripts lol.” What should change, and which version would the TEAS call most appropriate?

teach.h: Register: matching language to the moment
teach.body: Formally, register is the level of formality in language, chosen to fit the rhetorical context: the purpose of the message, its audience and its occasion or medium. Plain English: you would not text a dean the way you text your roommate, and you would not write a patient leaflet the way you write a lab report. On the TEAS, the right answer is the option that best fits the stated reader and purpose, not the one that sounds most impressive.

children.label: Occasion / medium
children.sub: email, report, text, brochure, essay, speech

teach.caption: Every register question names at least one of these. Underline it before reading the options.
Formal emails include messages to instructors, employers, admissions offices and officials.

teach.body: Formal does not mean complicated. A patient-education handout should use plain language: short sentences, everyday words and definitions for any needed term (“high blood pressure” rather than “hypertension”). Technical terms are right for a report to clinicians, who share that vocabulary. The test is always the reader: would this person understand it at once and take it seriously?

Nursing applicant Destiny Clark drafts an email to the admissions director: “Hey! So my college is being super slow with transcripts lol. Can u give me like 2 more days? Thx!!” The purpose (a request) is clear, but the register fails the audience: a greeting fit for friends, slang (super slow, like), text-speak (lol, u, thx) and double exclamation points. An admissions director may judge the applicant, not just the request.

“Dear Dr. Morales: I am writing to request a two-day extension on the transcript deadline. My college has not yet sent my official transcript, although I submitted the request on March 2. Thank you for considering this request. Sincerely, Destiny Clark.” Formal greeting, complete sentences, the request stated plainly in the first line, a reason, and a courteous close. It is formal without being stiff.

head: Context
Best register
rows: Email to an instructor or employer
Text to a friend or classmate

items: Underline the audience and purpose in the question stem.
For formal contexts, eliminate options with slang, text-speak, emojis or casual contractions.
For lay readers, eliminate options full of jargon or inflated words.
Eliminate polite options that never state what the message is for.
Choose the option that is clear, respectful and fits that reader.

teach.text: Three classic traps: picking the most academic-sounding option for a lay audience (jargon), picking a friendly but slangy option for a formal context, and picking a polite option that is so vague it never makes the request. The best answer fits the reader AND achieves the purpose.

items: Rhetorical context = purpose + audience + occasion or medium.
Formal: complete sentences, precise words, few contractions, no slang, text-speak or emojis.
Informal is right only for casual contexts such as texts and notes to friends.
Lay readers need plain language; specialists can handle technical terms.
The best option fits the stated reader and clearly achieves the stated purpose.

summary: You can now identify the purpose, audience and occasion of a message and choose formal, informal or plain-language wording to match. You can also reject options that are slangy, jargon-heavy, inflated or too vague to do their job.

A.q: Jalen is emailing his anatomy instructor to ask for a copy of the lab rubric. Which sentence is most appropriate?
options: Hey, can u send me the lab rubric thing when u get a sec?
Could you please send me a copy of the lab rubric?
I would be most humbly grateful should you deign to send it.
I was just wondering about some stuff for the lab, if that's okay.
A.why: It is polite, standard and states the exact request, which fits an email to an instructor.

whyNot.0: Text-speak (u) and casual phrasing (thing, a sec) are too informal for an instructor.
whyNot.2: Inflated, overly formal wording (humbly grateful, deign) sounds unnatural and never names the rubric.
whyNot.3: Vague: it never says what Jalen actually wants.

A.q: A leaflet for adults newly diagnosed with high blood pressure needs one sentence explaining the condition. Which is most appropriate?
options: Hypertension is a sustained elevation of systemic arterial pressure.
High BP is no joke, so get those numbers down ASAP!
Your BP is basically way too high, which is bad news.
High blood pressure means blood pushes too hard on artery walls.
A.why: Plain, accurate everyday words suit a lay audience reading a patient leaflet.

whyNot.0: Technical jargon (sustained elevation, systemic arterial) is unclear to lay readers.
whyNot.1: Slang (no joke, ASAP) and an exclamation point are too casual for health information.
whyNot.2: Slang (basically, way too high, bad news) is unprofessional and alarming.

A.q: Which sentence is most appropriate for a formal academic essay?
options: You'll see that sleep has a big effect on your test scores.
Sleep is super important if you want to ace your tests, no doubt.
Research suggests that sleep strongly affects test performance.
I totally think getting sleep is the key to killing it on tests.
A.why: Objective, third-person, precise wording fits a formal academic essay.

whyNot.0: Second person (you) and a contraction (You'll) are informal for an academic essay.
whyNot.1: Slang (super, ace, no doubt) and second person (you) are too informal.
whyNot.3: Slang (totally, killing it) and a casual first-person opinion do not fit.

B.q: Which message is most appropriate to text a close classmate about meeting to study?
options: Want to meet at the library at 6 to go over the cardio unit?
I hereby request your attendance at a study session this evening.
Pursuant to our course schedule, a review session is proposed.
Dear Classmate: Please confirm attendance at 1800 hours today.
B.why: A friendly, informal question with the key details (place, time, topic) suits a text to a friend.

whyNot.1: Stiff, legal-sounding formality (hereby request) is out of place in a text to a friend.
whyNot.2: Bureaucratic wording (pursuant to) does not fit a casual text.
whyNot.3: A formal salutation and 1800 hours are needlessly formal for a classmate.

B.q: Marisol is writing to her supervisor to request a schedule change. Which sentence best achieves her purpose?
options: I hope you are doing well and that the week is going smoothly.
Switch my March 14 shift or I can't come in, sorry!
I would like to switch my March 14 shift to March 16.
There may be some issues with my schedule at some point soon.
B.why: It states the exact request politely and directly, which is the purpose of the message.

whyNot.0: Polite, but it never makes the request, so it fails the purpose.
whyNot.1: Demanding and informal; the tone is wrong for a supervisor.
whyNot.3: Vague: no dates and no actual request.

B.q: Which feature would be LEAST appropriate in a personal statement for a nursing program?
options: First-person narration
Specific volunteer examples
Varied sentence lengths
Slang such as “super chill”
B.why: A personal statement is a formal document, so slang is inappropriate.

whyNot.0: First person is expected in a personal statement, because applicants are telling their own stories.
whyNot.1: Specific examples strengthen a personal statement.
whyNot.2: Varied sentence lengths are a mark of strong formal writing.

C.q: A hospital volunteer coordinator is writing a welcome letter to new volunteers aged 16 to 18. Which opening sentence is most appropriate?
options: Yo, welcome to the squad, you're gonna crush it!
Welcome! We are glad you joined our volunteer team.
Your onboarding will be executed per HR protocol 4.2.
Welcome, though we expect most of you won't last long.
C.why: Warm but standard English fits a young audience in a professional setting.

whyNot.0: Slang (yo, squad, gonna, crush it) is unprofessional even for teens.
whyNot.2: Cold, jargon-filled wording (onboarding, executed per protocol) does not welcome anyone.
whyNot.3: The tone is condescending and discouraging.

C.q: A nursing student is revising a sentence for a report that clinicians will read: “The patient's sugar was way high after lunch.” Which revision is most appropriate?
options: The patient's blood glucose was elevated after lunch.
The patient's sugar was super high after lunch.
The patient's sugar went through the roof after lunch.
Sadly, the poor patient's sugar was high after lunch.
C.why: Clinicians expect precise technical terms (blood glucose, elevated) and an objective tone.

whyNot.1: Super high is slang and imprecise.
whyNot.2: Went through the roof is an idiom, too casual for a clinical report.
whyNot.3: Emotional words (sadly, poor) are not objective, and sugar is imprecise.

C.q: A city health department is posting on social media about a free flu shot clinic for the general public. Which sentence is most appropriate?
options: Immunoprophylaxis against influenza is offered Saturday.
Flu shots r free Sat, so pull up or whatever lol.
Free flu shots: Saturday, 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., Lincoln Library.
Some health events may happen soon, so stay tuned for details.
C.why: Plain language with the key facts (what, when, where) suits the general public and the purpose.

whyNot.0: Jargon (immunoprophylaxis) is unclear to the general public, and it omits the time and place.
whyNot.1: Text-speak (r, lol) is unprofessional for a government agency.
whyNot.3: Too vague to inform anyone about the clinic.

reteach.title: Dress for the occasion
reteach.question: You would not wear pajamas to a job interview or a suit to the beach. How is choosing words like choosing clothes?

blocks.body: Formal register is the interview suit: complete sentences, precise words, no slang. Informal register is weekend clothes: contractions, casual words, fine with friends. Plain language is a clean uniform: simple and clear so anyone can understand it, like a patient leaflet. Wearing the wrong outfit does not change who you are, but it changes how the reader judges you and whether your message lands.

head: Occasion
Outfit
Word choice
rows: Dear Dr. Morales, I am requesting ...

blocks.text: Overdressing is also wrong: a tuxedo at a picnic (“Pursuant to our plans...” in a text to a friend) misses the occasion just as badly as pajamas at an interview.

explain.body: Every message has a purpose (inform, persuade, request, instruct, entertain), an audience and an occasion or medium. Identify all three before judging the language.

head: Purpose
Sample message
rows: Get your flu shot this week.

test.q: A leaflet that explains, step by step, how to use an inhaler is written mainly to:
options: entertain
persuade
request
instruct
test.why: Step-by-step directions teach the reader how to do something, so the purpose is to instruct.

whyNot.0: Nothing in a how-to leaflet is meant to amuse.
whyNot.1: It does not try to change the reader's opinion; it shows how to do a task.
whyNot.2: It does not ask the reader for anything.

explain.body: Formal writing uses complete sentences, precise standard vocabulary, an objective tone and few contractions. It avoids slang, text-speak, emojis and direct address in academic writing.

test.q: Which sentence fits a formal lab report?
options: The results were kinda surprising, tbh.
The results were unexpected.
The results totally blew us away.
You won't believe these results!
test.why: Precise, objective standard English fits a formal report.

whyNot.0: Kinda and tbh are slang and text-speak.
whyNot.2: Totally blew us away is slang.
whyNot.3: Second person, a contraction and an exclamation point are informal.

explain.body: Informal register is appropriate only when the audience is close and the occasion is casual: texts and notes to friends, family or classmates.

test.q: In which situation is an informal register most appropriate?
options: A text to your roommate
A scholarship application essay
An email to a dean
A lab report
test.why: A text to a roommate is a casual message to someone close, so informal language fits.

whyNot.1: A scholarship essay is a formal document judged by a committee.
whyNot.2: A dean is a professional audience that calls for formal language.
whyNot.3: A lab report is formal, objective academic writing.

explain.body: Jargon is specialized vocabulary. It is efficient among specialists but confusing for the general public, who need everyday words and defined terms.

test.q: Which term should replace “analgesic” in a leaflet for the general public?
options: NSAID agent
antinociceptive
pain reliever
analgesic drug
test.why: Pain reliever is the everyday term a lay reader understands at once.

whyNot.0: NSAID is a technical abbreviation most lay readers will not know.
whyNot.1: Antinociceptive is even more technical than the original word.
whyNot.3: It keeps the jargon word analgesic, so nothing becomes clearer.
